blocks.text: Once you have written an MCP server, you need a fast way to check that it actually works.
Writing a whole client application just to test one tool call is slow and wasteful.
The MCP Inspector solves this by giving you a ready made window into any server.
1. What the MCP Inspector Is

blocks.alt: A developer uses the Inspector UI to talk to a local MCP server

blocks.text: The MCP Inspector is an official, standalone developer tool maintained alongside the protocol itself.
It connects to any MCP server, not just ones you wrote, and lets you explore it interactively.
You see its tools, resources, and prompts laid out in a browser tab, ready to click and try.
2. Installing and Launching the Inspector
You do not install the Inspector as a project dependency, you run it directly with npx.
Point it at the command that starts your server, and it launches both pieces together.

code.content:
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node build/index.js

# or a python server
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py

blocks.text: The command prints a local URL, usually on port 6274, that opens the Inspector in your browser.
3. Connecting to a Local Server Under Development

blocks.alt: The Inspector connects directly to a server under active development

blocks.text: Behind the scenes the Inspector actually spawns your server process using the command you gave it.
That means it always talks to the exact code sitting on your disk right now.
Change a handler, restart the Inspector, and you are testing the new version immediately.

blocks.title: Fast feedback loop
blocks.content: Because the Inspector spawns your real server, there is no mock layer between you and your actual code, so bugs show up exactly as a host would see them.

blocks.text: 4. The Inspector Interface: Tabs Overview
Once connected, the Inspector splits into tabs, each covering one part of the protocol surface.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tab","What it shows"],"rows":[["Tools","Every tool the server exposes, with its input schema"],["Resources","Every resource and resource template the server offers"],["Prompts","Every prompt template and its expected arguments"],["Notifications","Server initiated messages like progress or log lines"],["History","A running log of every request and response sent so far"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Browsing Tools
The Tools tab lists every tool name and description your server registered.
Selecting a tool renders its input schema as an actual form, one field per parameter.
This is the fastest way to confirm your schema is what you think it is.
6. Manually Calling a Tool and Reading the Response

blocks.alt: A developer manually calls a tool and reads the raw response back

blocks.text: Fill in the generated form fields and press the call button, no code required.
Say your server exposes a search_notes tool, you can try it right from the browser.
The response panel shows the returned content exactly as your handler produced it.
If a tool throws an error, the Inspector shows that error clearly instead of a blank result.
7. Browsing and Reading Resources
The Resources tab lists static resources and any templated resource patterns.
For a template, the Inspector lets you fill in the placeholder and fetch a real instance.
You read the returned content directly, confirming the resource behaves as documented.
8. Browsing Prompts
The Prompts tab lists every prompt template along with its declared arguments.
Filling in the arguments and running the prompt shows the exact message list it produces.
This is useful for checking wording before wiring the prompt into a real host.
9. Viewing Raw JSON-RPC Messages

blocks.alt: The Inspector shows the raw JSON-RPC messages flowing underneath

blocks.text: Underneath every button click, the Inspector is sending real JSON-RPC over the wire.
The History tab lets you expand any call and see the exact request that was sent.
Seeing the raw envelope matters when a client library seems to disagree with your server.
10. Debugging With Notifications and Logs
Some servers send notifications outside the normal request and response cycle.
Progress updates and log messages both land in the Notifications tab as they arrive.
This lets you confirm a long running tool is actually reporting progress correctly.
11. Inspector vs Writing a Test Client

blocks.alt: Using the Inspector is compared against writing a custom test client

blocks.text: You could always write a small script using the SDK client class to call a tool.
That works, but it means writing and maintaining code just to check something manually.
The Inspector gives you the same access with zero code and a much faster loop.

items: A custom client needs to be written, run, and edited every time you want to try something new
The Inspector already understands the full protocol, so every tool, resource, and prompt is just a click away
Raw message inspection in a custom client means adding your own logging, the Inspector already shows it
A custom client is still worth writing later, but only once you need automated, repeatable tests

blocks.text: 12. Where the Inspector Fits in Your Workflow
Most developers reach for the Inspector immediately after writing a new tool or resource.
It becomes the manual smoke test you run before ever connecting a real host application.
Once things look right in the Inspector, you move on to wiring the server into an actual assistant.
13. Connecting to a Remote or Already Running Server

blocks.alt: The Inspector connects to a remote server that is already running

blocks.text: The Inspector is not limited to servers it spawns itself.
You can also point it at a server already running over HTTP by supplying its URL.
This is handy for checking a server deployed somewhere else without touching its source.
14. Configuration and Environment Variables
Some servers need environment variables, an API key or a database path, to start correctly.
The Inspector lets you pass these in through its connection panel before you ever call a tool.
15. Known Limitations to Keep in Mind

blocks.alt: A manual tool is compared against automated testing for its known limitations

blocks.text: The Inspector is a manual tool, it will not replace an automated test suite for regressions.
It also is not meant to be exposed publicly, it assumes a trusted developer sitting in front of it.

blocks.title: Local tool, not a deployment target
blocks.content: The Inspector is meant for your own machine during development. Never expose its port to the open internet.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Say you just finished a small tasks server with one tool called add_task.
The browser opens, the Tools tab shows add_task, and you fill in a title field.
Pressing call sends a tools/call request and the response panel shows your confirmation text.
Expanding that entry in History shows the exact JSON-RPC request and response pair.
In under a minute you have proven the tool works, with no test client written at all.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the server must actually build or compile first, so the Inspector spawns a stale binary
Assuming the Inspector edits your server, it only calls what already exists, it changes nothing
Leaving the Inspector reachable on a shared network instead of running it only on localhost
Skipping the History tab and missing a malformed JSON-RPC message that explains a confusing bug
Testing only the happy path and never trying invalid arguments to see how errors are reported
Treating the Inspector as a substitute for real automated tests once the server is stable

blocks.text: Practice
Take any MCP server you have already written and launch it with the Inspector.
Call one tool with valid arguments, then call it again with a missing required field.
Compare the two raw JSON-RPC responses in the History tab and note exactly how the error differs.
Key Takeaway
The MCP Inspector turns a silent, code only protocol into something you can see and click through.
Reach for it first, before writing any client code, whenever you need to check a server by hand.
